title: Public-Records Vault for City Employee AI Chats
one_liner: Capture, retain, redact and produce every government employee's AI prompt and response as the public record it legally is.
customer: City clerks, county records officers and city attorneys at cities of 20-300K people that just rolled out AI assistants to staff.
problem: Every prompt and output from a government employee is likely a public record subject to retention schedules and open-records requests. Cities are turning AI on in Chattanooga-style rollouts with no retention system. A single request from a journalist could force manual digging through vendor logs the city may not control.
solution: Browser extension and API proxy that captures AI interactions across tools, tags them to retention schedules, redacts exempt content (personnel, law enforcement, attorney-client), and generates one-click productions for open-records requests. Litigation-hold support included.
why_now: Local AI adoption is now real, with police, school and bus-routing deployments. GenAI.mil users have built more than 100k agents. Records lawyers are starting to warn, and the first open-records fights over chatbot logs will land in 2026-27.
revenue_model: $8-40K per year per city by headcount, plus e-discovery production fees. Reseller channel via records-management vendors.
non_obvious_insight: AI adoption creates a records problem before it creates a safety problem. The clerk, not the CIO, has a legal deadline and a small budget line for exactly this.
first_30_days: Talk to 10 city clerks and 3 state records associations. Build the capture extension for two chat tools and a retention-schedule mapper. Pilot free with 2 cities that have announced AI programs, and convert on the first open-records request.

title: Workforce Pell Approval-as-a-Service
one_liner: A fixed-fee desk that turns a college's short-program idea into an approved Workforce Pell application with employer-demand evidence, outcomes math and state sign-off.
customer: Community colleges, technical colleges, proprietary trade schools, workforce boards and apprenticeship sponsors with 8-15 week programs (EMT, CDL, welding, medical assistant, phlebotomy).
problem: Workforce Pell launched July 1, 2026 but only 5 programs were approved by September 22. Colleges call the process hard and complicated. They lack capacity to prove employer demand, calculate outcome tests and obtain governor and state workforce-board sign-off, while vocational-heavy public two-years grew 11.7% in Spring 2025.
solution: Done-for-you application packages: a local labor-demand memo with job-posting data and employer letters, cost-versus-earnings math, outcomes tracking setup for completion and placement, and state-by-state approval navigation. Design programs to be apprenticeship-linked, because registered apprenticeships with college instruction auto-qualify as in-demand and up to 49% of instruction can be outsourced to employers or unions.
why_now: The program is three months old, states are still building approval procedures, and the first approvals came from Iowa Central (EMT) and Ivy Tech (medical assistant). First movers get enrollment for the 2027 terms.
revenue_model: $12-30k per program application plus $500-1,500 a month for outcomes reporting; optional success fee.
non_obvious_insight: The constraint is not curriculum or students but making programs legible to regulators. Approval capacity is the scarce resource, so whoever standardizes the evidence package becomes the gatekeeper's best friend.
first_30_days: Read the statute and guidance, and pick two states with active approvals. Offer 3 community colleges a fixed price with a partial success guarantee. Publish a free checklist to pull leads from workforce boards.

title: Hatchery-Specific Phage Cocktails on Subscription
one_liner: A monthly service that isolates each shrimp hatchery's own Vibrio strains and ships a custom bacteriophage cocktail to kill them, so hatcheries can stop using antibiotics.
customer: Shrimp hatcheries and nurseries in Vietnam, India, Ecuador and Indonesia, plus the exporters and feed companies that buy their post-larvae and need antibiotic-free supply.
problem: Vibrio outbreaks (AHPND/EMS) wipe out whole hatchery batches. Antibiotics are banned in export markets, but residues keep turning up: a 2025 analysis attributes 43% of shrimp export rejections by the EU, US and Japan to chloramphenicol and nitrofuran residues, and 19 Indian consignments were rejected in 2025-26. Post-larvae pass through fragmented hatcheries and aggregators, so nobody can trace or fix the source. Generic probiotics and disinfectants work unevenly.
solution: A lab-in-a-box subscription. We sample water and biofilm each month and sequence and culture the local Vibrio isolates. We screen them against a curated phage library and ship a hatchery-specific cocktail as a water or feed additive. The cocktail is refreshed as strains drift, and later we add AI-designed phages. Each shipment comes with a residue-free 'clean seed' data pack that exporters and buyers can audit. Selling it in the feed-additive or probiotic regulatory class, not as a drug, keeps approval fast in most shrimp-producing countries.
why_now: Antibiotic bans (India's March 2025 notification banning chloramphenicol and nitrofurans in food-producing animals) are colliding with continued export rejections. Generative phage design became real in September 2025, when the Arc Institute and Stanford, using the Evo genome models, produced 16 viable AI-designed phage genomes from 302 candidates, later published in Science. Nanopore sequencing is cheap enough to run near ponds. Buyers now demand antibiotic-free attestations.
revenue_model: Subscription of roughly $400-1,500 per month per hatchery, scaled by tank volume, plus per-batch emergency cocktails at a premium. Exporters or feed companies pay a per-lot attestation fee. Longer term, license the phage library and drift dataset to feed and biosecurity companies.
non_obvious_insight: A phage is host-specific and keeps evolving with its target, so it works badly as a mass-market molecule and well as a perishable, local, continuously updated service. Big pharma cannot profitably do bespoke, and that is the wedge. The moat is the living library of regional strains and the resistance-drift dataset, and the hatchery is the chokepoint of the whole seed supply chain, so clean seed pays off downstream.
first_30_days: Partner with one university phage lab in Vietnam, India or Ecuador. Offer 10 hatcheries free strain-isolation reports to build the initial library, and pitch each hatchery a $500-per-month paid pilot. Ask one export processor to sponsor 3 pilots to secure antibiotic-free seed for its supply chain.

title: Human Reach Audits for Newsletter and Podcast Sponsors
one_liner: Bot- and agent-scrubbed reach certificates that let honest newsletters and podcasts charge sponsors for verified human eyeballs.
customer: Newsletter and podcast operators with $5k-200k/month in sponsorship revenue on the sell side, and B2B sponsors, creator agencies and marketplaces on the buy side.
problem: Cloudflare's CEO says bots are about 20% of traffic and will exceed human traffic by 2027, with agents hitting about 1,000x more sites than a human. Opens, clicks and downloads increasingly come from scanners and AI assistants, not people. B2B sponsors buying through marketplaces such as Passionfroot and Agentio will see CPA misses and disputes, and start discounting all creators. Honest operators are hurt most.
solution: Connect to the newsletter platform and podcast host logs (Beehiiv, Ghost, Mailchimp, Libsyn, Buzzsprout). Classify every open, click and download as human, scanner or agent using timing, IP ranges, user-agent patterns and hidden honeypot links. Issue a 'Verified Human Reach' certificate with methodology and monitor it monthly, plus a sponsor-facing verify link. Later, offer pricing per verified-human click.
why_now: The bot-share trend is now being stated by infrastructure CEOs, B2B creator marketplaces are scaling (Passionfroot $15M, Agentio $40M), and reader-side detection has entered the mainstream through Substack's Pangram scan. Sponsors are getting more skeptical this budget cycle.
revenue_model: $199-499 per audit, $99/month monitoring, marketplace API fees per certificate, and a performance fee on verified-human click pricing.
non_obvious_insight: The authenticity gap that moves money is not in the content but in the audience. Sponsors buy human attention, and a certificate lets honest creators earn a premium rather than being averaged down.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 sponsor-funded newsletters via Beehiiv and Substack communities and offer a free 'what percent of your clicks are bots' scan in exchange for publishing an anonymized benchmark. Sell certificates before their next media-kit refresh, and pitch two B2B marketplaces or agencies.

title: Settlement Passports for Florida High-Rise Condos
one_liner: A satellite-radar settlement history for every Florida condo tower, sold as the cheap first page of the milestone-inspection and reserve-study file.
customer: Florida condo associations and the licensed engineers and property managers who run their milestone inspections and structural integrity reserve studies; secondary buyers are master-policy underwriters, lenders and buyers' agents doing condo diligence.
problem: Carriers want structural documents before they bind a master policy, SIRS and milestone inspections are mandatory for 3+ story buildings, and special assessments run $50K-$200K+ per unit. Boards cannot tell whether their building is stable or sinking until an engineer bills for scoping. A 2024 University of Miami InSAR study found 35 Miami Beach to Sunny Isles buildings subsiding 2-8 cm over 2016-2023, and no commercial product packages this for boards.
solution: Process free Sentinel-1 radar (2015 onward), ESA archive radar for the 1990s-2010s, and newly public NISAR L-band data into a per-building vertical-motion trend. Add differential tilt across the footprint and a comparison against neighbours built on similar fill. Deliver a 3-page Settlement Passport plus a monitoring feed, positioned as a screening indicator that sharpens inspection scope, with an engineer partner signing off. It is not a substitute for the inspection.
why_now: Florida's post-Surfside SB 4-D inspection and reserve-study mandates are now enforced and carriers demand documents. NISAR L-band data has been free through ASF since the July 20, 2026 public release, adding to the Sentinel-1 record. Peer-reviewed proof that InSAR resolves individual Miami towers exists but has not been productized. Reinsurance is softening while condo retail insurance is still squeezed.
revenue_model: $900-$2,500 per building for the initial passport and $300/yr for monitoring. Wholesale price of about $400 to engineering firms who bundle it into SIRS work. $100/building/yr portfolio contracts for management companies.
non_obvious_insight: InSAR is treated as an academic or pipeline-monitoring tool, but the buyer with a legal deadline and a real budget is a condo board that must assemble a structural file. Persistent-scatterer InSAR works best on concrete high-rises, the exact asset at issue. The 10-30 year archive can also show a building has been stable for decades, which makes it a positive underwriting asset for the many buildings that are fine, not just a warning label.
first_30_days: Run the free Sentinel-1 stack for about 400 buildings on the Miami-Dade and Broward barrier islands. Offer one free passport to each of 15 engineering firms and 5 management companies, and sign 2 engineers as resellers. Then charge the first 10 boards facing reserve-study or insurance-renewal deadlines.

title: Cool-Hours Slot Exchange for Tour Operators
one_liner: Forecast-driven heat re-scheduling for tour operators, plus a marketplace that sells 7am and 8pm venue slots, turning the coolest hours of the day into a priced, allocated resource.
customer: Independent ground-tour operators, destination management companies and cruise shore-excursion desks (10-200 guides) in Athens, Rome, Seville, Marrakech, Petra and Kyoto. The supply side is private venues (wineries, palazzi, small museums, cooking schools) with unused early and late capacity.
problem: Overtourism policy fixates on fees and caps, but the real crush is temporal: coaches, lunch and check-out times funnel everyone into 10:00-15:00, exactly when heat peaks. Operators cancel and refund ad hoc, guides carry heat-illness risk, and there is no record of duty-of-care decisions for insurers under package-travel liability. Meanwhile venues sit empty at dawn and dusk.
solution: Three layers. (1) A scheduler that ingests 5-day heat-stress (WBGT/UTCI) forecasts and the operator's tour book, rebuilds itineraries (dawn starts, indoor midday, evening loops), messages guests in their language and re-checks availability. (2) A time-stamped duty-of-care log (decisions, water and shade stops, guest health flags) exportable to insurers. (3) A slot exchange where venues list early and late timed entries at a premium and operators buy allotments in bulk. Venues get demand data to justify extended hours.
why_now: Summer 2026 Europe saw record heat and a reported provisional death toll near 38,000 (secondary source), pushing operators and regulators toward heat rules. Destinations are moving from fees to allocation: Venice's day-tripper fee reportedly did not cut numbers, while Mount Fuji's hard 4,000/day cap plus fee works. Allocation needs tooling nobody has built. Margins are squeezed by jet-fuel-driven cost increases, so avoiding refunds matters.
revenue_model: EUR 199-499 per month SaaS per operator (tiered by guide count), 4-6% take on slot-exchange GMV, and paid analytics for venues and DMOs ($10-30K per year).
non_obvious_insight: Heat converts overtourism from a space problem into a time problem, and cool hours are the unpriced scarce commodity. They can be allocated like airport slots. Operators are natural demand aggregators, so a small team can win venue supply by promising bulk purchase. The duty-of-care log is what gets insurers interested, because it cuts claim exposure.
first_30_days: Interview 20 Athens and Rome operators about summer 2026 heat-day losses. Build the scheduler as a WhatsApp plus Google Sheets workflow on open forecast data for 5 pilot operators. Get 5 private venues to commit to 08:00 or 19:30 allotments. Demo at WTM London (Nov 2026) and FITUR Madrid (Jan 2027), and convert pilots to paid before the 2027 season.

title: ITAR-Safe Identity for New-Space Startups
one_liner: An identity layer that proves a new hire is real, where they actually are and whether they may legally see spacecraft technical data, then feeds that attribute straight into SSO and PLM access controls.
customer: Series A-C launch, satellite and defense-space startups (50-500 staff) and their sub-tier machine shops and avionics suppliers, reached through space-focused investors, accelerators and SpaceWERX/SBIR cohorts. Buyers are the head of security or compliance and the CFO.
problem: Space startups are hiring at breakneck speed, with remote engineers and contractors, into a Golden Dome-driven market (cost estimate raised to $185B) and nine-figure funding rounds. Giving a foreign person access to technical data is an ITAR export violation, and North Korean IT-worker schemes have reached 70 to 100+ US companies. Standard IDV proves someone is real, not whether they are a US person, and HR and ATS tools do not carry export-control eligibility as an access attribute. Fake suppliers and counterfeit parts add a second exposure.
solution: (1) Verify person and US-person status using document and injection-resistant liveness (partner with an existing IDV vendor rather than building it). (2) Check presence over time (VPN and laptop-farm signals). (3) Write 'US person, permitted data categories' into Okta or Entra groups and PLM and repo permissions through SCIM. (4) Supplier onboarding with KYB, sanctions and counterfeit-part red flags. (5) An auditor-ready evidence pack for CMMC Level 2 assessments and export-compliance reviews.
why_now: The DoD's CMMC rollout reaches its second phase on 10 Nov 2026, when third-party Level 2 certification starts appearing in contracts, and small suppliers are scrambling. North Korean worker prosecutions in Apr and May 2026 put hiring fraud on boards' agendas, while 3-second voice cloning and virtual-camera injection attacks defeat casual video interviews.
revenue_model: $60-120 per verified person per year, $1-3K per month platform fee, and $250 per supplier onboarding. Add a paid $2K 'ITAR access audit' as an entry product.
non_obvious_insight: In space the compliance object is not employee identity but nationality-scoped access to technical data. The unbuilt gap is attribute-based access control fed by identity proof into CAD and PLM systems. These startups fear DDTC and DoD audits and investor diligence more than hackers, so they buy compliance evidence rather than security.
first_30_days: Build a 'verified US person to Okta group' integration on an off-the-shelf IDV API. Sell a $2K ITAR access audit (export the Drive, GitHub and PLM permission lists and flag foreign-person exposures) to 5 startups via investor and accelerator introductions in Colorado Springs, Los Angeles and Huntsville. Convert audits to per-seat subscriptions before the Nov 2026 CMMC milestone.

title: Dementia Desk: Ex-Aide Call Center for Banks
one_liner: A remote call-center pod staffed by former dementia aides, taking the confused, repeat and possibly scammed callers that credit unions and utilities cannot handle.
customer: Credit unions ($200M-$3B assets), regional banks, municipal and regional utilities, and pharmacy chains' member-service teams. The compliance or member-experience officer signs. Medicare Advantage plan call centers are the second wave.
problem: Front-line agents are scored on handle time. A caller with dementia asks the same question nine times, fails the security questions, insists a dead husband is in the room, or is being coached by a scammer sitting beside them. Agents correct them, hang up or escalate. That distresses the caller, costs the institution money and produces fraud losses. Free training exists (AARP BankSafe videos), but nobody takes the hard calls.
solution: A warm-transfer line. The agent presses a button on any call that sounds impaired and a Dementia Desk specialist takes over within seconds. Specialists are ex-aides with 5-15 years in dementia care. They use the aide toolkit: join the caller's reality, don't correct, redirect, never argue about facts, and verify later with the trusted contact. They can also tell when a second voice is coaching. Each call ends with a structured note: risk flag, trusted-contact action, card freeze, callback plan. The service also hands the institution documented staff training for the Senior Safe Act.
why_now: The oldest boomers turn 80 in 2026, so vulnerable callers are rising fast. AI voice-clone scams against elders spiked in 2025-26. The Senior Safe Act (12 USC 3423) grants a bank immunity for reporting suspected exploitation only if the staff were trained and the training is documented. Home care aides are leaving the field with back injuries and low pay, and remote work at $20-24 per hour is a real second career for them.
revenue_model: $9-14 per handled contact with a $2,000 monthly minimum. A $4 per employee per year Senior Safe Act training add-on. Later, a per-account fee for a 'trusted contact enrollment' outbound program that reduces fraud losses.
non_obvious_insight: The problem is not detection. Institutions already know who's confused. The problem is that nobody on the phone knows what to do next and every training video is passive. The scarce skill is de-escalating cognitively impaired adults, and the only people who have it at scale are underpaid home aides. This turns the labor supply that home care has been losing into a premium BPO product, and it gives aides a career path off their spines.
first_30_days: Recruit 8 ex-aides from CNA and HHA school alumni groups and caregiver Facebook groups. Write a 12-page call playbook from their own scripts. Offer two local credit unions a free 60-day pilot: agents warm-transfer any call they flag to a Google Voice line the pod answers, with a monthly report of fraud saves. Charge from month three. Ask the state credit union league to host a 30-minute 'confused caller' webinar as the lead source.

title: Independent Service Roll-Up for Lab Robots
one_liner: Roll up independent service shops for liquid handlers and lab robots, using remote diagnostics and pooled parts to undercut OEM contracts for squeezed academic cores and CROs.
customer: Academic core facilities, small biotechs and CROs running Hamilton, Tecan, Beckman, Agilent and Opentrons fleets; later autonomous-lab operators who need uptime.
problem: NIH turbulence (a grant-cap proposal, stripped grants-staff protections, K99 visa limits) squeezes core budgets. OEM service contracts typically run about 8-12% of list price per year (an estimate) and OEMs prioritize pharma customers. Layoffs at biotechs and tool vendors free skilled field engineers. Downtime costs more as labs become automated.
solution: Flat-fee per-robot subscriptions at 30-40% below OEM, remote log ingestion with AI triage of error codes, a shared refurbished-parts pool sourced from wind-downs, and uptime guarantees. Acquire 2-4 small independent service shops at 3-5x EBITDA to get technicians and customers.
why_now: STAT tracks ongoing NIH instability. Biopharma layoffs (15,000+) and shuttered labs supply both engineers and used parts. More robots are being installed for AI-directed workflows.
revenue_model: $8-30k per robot per year at 55-65% gross margin on contracts, plus parts and time-and-materials, plus multiple arbitrage on acquired shops.
non_obvious_insight: Automation's bottleneck is uptime, not capability. Agent-run labs make downtime costlier, and robot telemetry lets an independent shop beat the OEM on mean time to repair. Wind-down biotechs are a parts supply the OEMs do not control.
first_30_days: Hire 2 ex-OEM field engineers. Sign 5-8 academic cores in one metro at introductory pricing. Buy used spares from wind-downs. Build a log-parsing dashboard for Hamilton and Tecan error logs.

title: Rails Weather: Live Nigerian Payment Reliability Index
one_liner: An independent, always-on measurement of which bank-to-bank transfers are actually working right now, sold as an API and SLA evidence.
customer: Payment service providers, aggregators and mid-size fintechs that route transfers; large merchants and marketplaces; fintech partnership desks that need evidence in disputes with sponsor banks. Consumers get a free status page.
problem: Every Nigerian fintech founder knows transfer success varies by bank pair and hour. It drops at month-end salary rushes, on Friday evenings, and during weekend core-banking upgrades. Worst of all is the 'pending' or 'successful but not credited' limbo. Nobody publishes independent data, bank status pages are unreliable, and fintechs keep private dashboards. Users cope by keeping 3-5 accounts and switching to whichever works, and merchants insist on POS because they distrust transfers. Small fintechs cannot prove to sponsor banks or regulators where the failures originate.
solution: Run automated, staggered probe transfers between the team's own accounts across the top 10-15 banks and fintechs, measuring success rate, time-to-credit and the pending-then-resolve rate. Only the transfer fee is lost, since the money returns to a team account. Publish a free public status page for reach. Sell a routing-intelligence API (best rail or account right now, expected delay), monthly SLA-evidence reports, and alerts. Later, add a privacy-safe data co-op in which fintechs contribute anonymised outcome counts in exchange for deeper, real-time bank-pair data.
why_now: CBN moved 2026 into an enforcement year, with open banking, APP-fraud and failed-transaction rules all coming due together. Fintechs now have to show measured reliability, not just assert it. POS and transfer volume has exploded (5.9 million active POS terminals; N10.5 trillion of POS transactions in Q1 2025 alone). Cheap serverless probing and LLM-written incident summaries make a two-person team viable.
revenue_model: API subscription tiers of about N250k to N3m per month depending on volume. Enterprise SLA and dispute-evidence reports at N1-5m per report. A data-co-op membership fee. A sponsored 'Nigeria Payments Index' report for banks and media.
non_obvious_insight: The key metric is time-to-credit and the size of the ambiguous-pending bucket, not success rate. Banks report 'success' at the API level while customers wait hours. Independent measurement is also the only neutral evidence in the fight between sponsor banks and fintechs over who caused a failure, and neither side can publish it themselves.
first_30_days: Open business accounts at 8-10 institutions. Write a probe scheduler that costs roughly N3m per month at a 15-minute cadence across about 100 pairs. Publish a public dashboard and a weekly 'worst bank pairs' thread that the fintech community shares. Offer 5 fintech CTOs a free 60-day API trial in return for feedback and sample failure logs. Convert the first 2-3 to paid once their own incident data lines up with the index.

title: Continuity Retainer for One-Licensee Funeral Homes
one_liner: Key-person insurance for funeral homes: a bench of pre-credentialed licensed directors and embalmers who step in within 24-48 hours when the owner is sick, burned out or gone, with a built-in path to succession.
customer: Independent and rural funeral homes with one or two licensed staff (roughly 30-150 calls a year), typically owner-operators aged 55-75. A second buyer is the family of an owner who has died or fallen ill and needs the home kept legal while it is sold.
problem: States require a licensed funeral director or manager-in-charge, and often a licensed embalmer, for an establishment to operate. The owner is on call 24/7/365 and hasn't had a real week off in years. One heart attack, surgery or burnout means the home cannot legally operate, families get funneled to the consolidator down the road, and a business built over three generations is sold at a distressed price. Informal 'relief director' phone lists exist, but there is no bench, no contract, no reciprocity or board paperwork handled, and no guarantee anyone answers at 3 a.m.
solution: Recruit retired and semi-retired licensed directors and embalmers, including many leaving consolidators, and pre-credential them in a target state cluster with background checks and reciprocity filings. Sell continuity retainers that guarantee a set number of coverage days a year (real vacations, weekends off) plus emergency activation within 24-48 hours at a day rate. The company handles the state-board notice of interim manager changes. A succession track lets an interim operator or next-generation licensed buyer convert into a partner or buyer with seller financing, so owners have an alternative to a roll-up.
why_now: Consolidation keeps shrinking the independent pool (SCI alone bought about 22 funeral homes and 2 cemeteries for roughly $101M in 2025). The licensed workforce is aging while mortuary-school pipelines are thin. Rising cremation lowers revenue per case, making full-time second hires unaffordable for small homes. Rural closures are creating 'funeral deserts'. Many states have passed occupational-license recognition laws that make multi-state relief staffing easier.
revenue_model: Retainer of $900-$2,000/month per home including N coverage days. Activation day rate of $800-$1,400 billed to the home, with a 25-30% margin over what the licensee is paid. Per-case fees for trade embalming and prep-room services. A 1-2% success fee on succession transactions.
non_obvious_insight: The real asset of an independent funeral home isn't the building, it's one license holder with a phone, and that is a single point of failure. Consolidators know it and wait. Owners will pay to sleep: this is a wellness and continuity product disguised as staffing, and its best feature is the succession pipeline it creates once a trusted operator is already inside the home.
first_30_days: Recruit eight retired licensed directors and embalmers through state association chapters and retiree groups. Check each state board's rules for temporary manager-in-charge designation. Pitch 20 one-licensee homes in two adjacent counties at a $1,200/month founding rate with a 'test weekend off' guarantee. Sign the first three, and run the first covered weekend within 30 days to produce a testimonial.

title: Federated Settlement-Benchmark Co-op for Small Firms
one_liner: Small plaintiff firms pool de-identified settlement outcomes from their practice-management systems to get case-value benchmarks that only insurers and big firms have today.
customer: Employment, wage-hour, personal-injury, med-mal and consumer boutiques with 1-15 attorneys. Later buyers are insurers, litigation funders and mediators purchasing aggregate indices.
problem: Verdict reporters capture only the few percent of cases that reach verdict, while nearly all money moves through confidential settlements. Insurers hold large claims databases, but plaintiff-side lawyers estimate value from gut feel and listservs. Frontier legal tools train on public opinions, not private outcomes, and outcome-priced legal work (as Norm Law sells) needs outcome data.
solution: With attorney approval, a practice-management connector extracts a handful of structured fields (claim type, venue, injury or violation class, damages band, procedural posture, time to resolution, fee outcome) into a secure aggregation layer with k-anonymity thresholds and differential privacy on outputs, no free text, and respect for confidentiality clauses. Members get instant valuation ranges and time-to-resolution, and aggregate indices are licensed to insurers and funders.
why_now: MCP connectors to practice-management systems are now real (8am: 60+ small firms in month one), privacy-preserving analytics tooling has matured, and outcome-based pricing plus a funded litigation-finance market create demand for outcome data.
revenue_model: Free for contributors (about 5 data points per quarter), $99-299/month for non-contributors, and $25-250k/year data licenses to insurers and funders.
non_obvious_insight: The most valuable legal dataset is in no court file. It sits in hundreds of thousands of small-firm ledgers. Firms will trade aggregated outcomes for benchmarks (as doctors do for registries), and Westlaw cannot copy that give-to-get flywheel because it has no view into settlements. Rule 1.6 and settlement confidentiality clauses are the main risk and need an ethics memo up front.
first_30_days: Run it manually first. Recruit 20 employment or wage-hour lawyers through a state bar section or NELA chapter, collect 10 de-identified data points each on a form, return a valuation sheet, and commission an ethics counsel memo. Then build the connector for one platform.

title: Disaster-Pause Rider for Small-Business Loans
one_liner: A parametric portfolio rider that lets CDFIs and credit unions automatically pause small-business and farm loan payments after a disaster, with the lender made whole by a pre-funded payout.
customer: Community lenders (CDFIs, credit unions, farm-credit and small-bank lenders) with $50-$500M loan books in disaster-exposed counties. The end beneficiaries are their small-business and consumer borrowers.
problem: After a hurricane, flood or fire, borrowers need a payment holiday, but lenders cannot afford to grant them automatically because the missed cash flow strains liquidity and reserves. Borrowers must plead, forbearance takes weeks of staff time, and many quietly default. CDFI funding is already fragile, so lenders hold back.
solution: A portfolio-level parametric policy keyed to county-level disaster declarations plus hazard footprints (wind swaths, flood extent, fire perimeters). It pays the lender the scheduled payments of borrowers in the footprint for 90-180 days. The loan documents carry a pre-approved 'automatic pause' clause, so borrowers never buy insurance. The lender markets 'storm-proof loans' and adds a rate rider of about 10-25 bps to pay for it. A software pause engine flags affected loans and sends notices.
why_now: Repeated large disasters and ongoing debate over shrinking or slowing federal disaster aid make private, fast liquidity more attractive. Federal support for CDFIs has been unsettled, so lenders want to protect portfolios. Parametric capacity is abundant and hazard-footprint data (NOAA swaths, flood extents) is public and precise.
revenue_model: MGA/brokerage fee of 15-20% on premium (roughly 25-60 bps of covered balance per year), plus a SaaS fee of $1,000-$5,000 per month for the pause-and-notice engine. Later, reinsurance placement and a data product on borrower resilience.
non_obvious_insight: After a disaster the scarce resource is lender liquidity, not rebuilding capital. A forbearance favor becomes a contractual right that costs the lender one clause, and distribution is the loan itself, so no borrower ever has to shop for or understand insurance.
first_30_days: Approach three Gulf Coast, Carolinas or California CDFIs and credit unions through CDFI trade networks. Write a one-page term sheet, price it from historical hazard footprints, and pilot on newly originated loans in one county. Pair with an MGA and a reinsurer, and target one signed letter of intent within 60 days.

title: TAKE IT DOWN Desk for Small Platforms
one_liner: Outsourced 48-hour notice-and-removal operations (intake, requester verification, adjudication, audit logs) for forums, hosts and indie social apps.
customer: Small and mid-size platforms with user-generated content (forums, image hosts, creator platforms, community apps, dating apps) that have no trust-and-safety staff, plus web hosts and their counsel.
problem: The FTC began enforcing the TAKE IT DOWN Act on 19 May 2026, wrote to 15 large platforms including Discord, Reddit and Automattic, and lists civil penalties of $53,088 per violation. Coverage reaches forums with user content. The 48-hour clock is real, but the request process is abusable, since false takedown notices can be weaponised, and platforms must verify that the requester is the depicted person without collecting more sensitive imagery.
solution: A hosted intake endpoint and a staffed desk. It offers identity-light requester verification (hash matching in the style of StopNCII), adjudication by trained reviewers with escalation, removal of known identical copies across the customer's site, an appeal and counter-notice path, and FTC-ready audit logs. Follow-the-sun contractors with wellness support provide coverage. Requires legal review per jurisdiction.
why_now: Enforcement started in May 2026, the FTC opened a complaint portal (TakeItDown.ftc.gov), and nonconsensual deepfake volume is rising. Small platforms cannot afford in-house teams, and the statute imposes a duty to act with no penalty for false requests.
revenue_model: $500-5k per month base plus $15-40 per resolved case, with enterprise SLAs.
non_obvious_insight: The statute mandates speed but not accuracy, so the operational risk is over-removal and abuse. The product is adjudication with a paper trail, not filtering, and the buyer's fear is an FTC letter, not a bad user.
first_30_days: Sell through forum-software hosting partners, web-hosting providers and indie creator platforms. Train a contractor pool in handling sensitive imagery and stand up intake for 10 pilot communities.

title: Dealer-Fee Decoder for Solar and Home Loans
one_liner: Use the auto F&I trick of hiding the buy-down in the price to expose the hidden 'dealer fee' inside 0% and low-rate solar, HVAC and roofing loans, then sell the evidence to consumer lawyers and the refinance to credit unions.
customer: First: consumer-protection and TILA law firms and legal aid running home-improvement and solar loan cases, at $49 to $149 per decoded loan. Second: credit unions and community banks that pay $150 to $300 per funded takeout loan.
problem: A '0% for 12 months' or '2.99% for 20 years' home-improvement loan is not cheap. The lender charges the contractor a discount or 'dealer fee' that commonly runs into double digits on promotional-rate loans, and the contractor recovers it by inflating the price for financed customers. It's the same mechanic as a dealer's reserve and buy-down in an auto F&I office. The borrower sees a low APR, cannot see the cash price they should have been quoted, and often pays a financed price 15 to 30% above the cash price. Minnesota's attorney general has sued GoodLeap over hidden fees folded into loan amounts, and complaints keep growing. Homeowners left with orphaned systems and no tax credit are a sympathetic and litigable group.
solution: A document-parsing decoder. The homeowner or lawyer uploads the contract, TILA disclosure and any competing cash quote. The tool extracts price, APR, term and any disclosed fee, and estimates the implied cash price and implied finance charge, meaning how much of the price is really interest. It compares this to a regional cash-price benchmark built from scraped quotes, contractor bid sites and permit data. It outputs a plain-language one-pager and a lawyer-grade exhibit for TILA and UDAP claims, then offers a credit-union takeout quote for the true payoff amount.
why_now: The federal residential solar tax credit for homeowner purchases ended after 2025, a wave of installers went bankrupt and left homeowners with loans on systems nobody services, state attorneys general have started suing, and the CFPB's federal enforcement has faded so states and private plaintiffs are the enforcement. Contingency-fee plaintiff firms are already advertising for GoodLeap-type cases and need faster intake screening.
revenue_model: Per-case fee from law firms ($49 to $149), a subscription for high-volume firms ($499 per month), and a bounty from credit unions for each funded refinance or takeout loan. Later, a compliance benchmark sold to honest contractors, to lenders and to regulators.
non_obvious_insight: Consumer advocates attack solar lenders as if the fee were unique to solar. A finance manager knows it is standard structure anywhere a merchant can 'buy down' a rate: the retail price quietly carries the cost. What law firms lack is not the theory but cheap, defensible, per-loan numbers to screen thousands of leads. The cash price counterfactual is the missing piece and the F&I mindset is exactly what tells you where to look for it.
first_30_days: Collect 200 real solar and HVAC loan document sets and cash-vs-financed quote pairs from public complaints, forums and two or three law-firm partners. Build the parser and implied-price model on them. Offer three plaintiff firms with active solar-loan intake 25 free screens each, then charge $99 a case. Meet two credit unions with home-improvement loan programs to agree a bounty for takeouts.

title: Wind Tunnel for Agent Markets and Pricing Collusion
one_liner: Simulate your pricing or buying agent against thousands of rival agents to see whether it drifts into tacit collusion, manipulation or first-offer traps before regulators or rivals do.
customer: Revenue-management and pricing-software vendors (hotels, multifamily, retail, insurance), marketplaces running agent-facing APIs, and the antitrust and compliance counsel who advise them. Regulators are a later customer.
problem: Academic work shows LLM pricing agents can converge on supracompetitive prices without communicating. Microsoft's Magentic Marketplace found agent buyers show strong first-proposal bias (a 10-30x advantage for response speed) and can be manipulated. Algorithmic pricing is already drawing antitrust suits and state laws, and nobody has a standard way to show a deployed pricing agent behaves competitively.
solution: Adapt the open-source Magentic Marketplace environment into a test harness with calibrated rival populations (LLM and RL agents). Run repeated-game tests measuring markups against a competitive baseline, information-leakage tests, and manipulation and first-offer sensitivity. Deliver an algorithmic pricing conduct report plus guardrails (randomization, no shared non-public data, price-parity limits) and re-test when the underlying model changes.
why_now: Agentic repricing is spreading, algorithmic-pricing enforcement is active, the simulation environment was open-sourced in late 2025, and models change every quarter so one-off audits go stale.
revenue_model: $40-$150k per audit, $5-$15k/month re-test subscriptions, and law-firm seat licenses.
non_obvious_insight: You cannot inspect intent inside a model, but you can test behavior in a sandbox economy. Like crash tests for cars, a standardized, reproducible test gives defendants a documented duty-of-care defense and gives regulators a common yardstick.
first_30_days: Adapt Magentic Marketplace to a hospitality-pricing scenario and write a methodology note. Approach 3 antitrust boutiques and 3 revenue-management vendors, and sell a $25k pilot audit.

title: Immunogenicity Screens for De Novo Proteins
one_liner: A fast, low-cost HLA-diverse T-cell screen and de-immunize-and-retest loop built for AI-designed proteins that have no natural template to humanize.
customer: AI protein-design startups and pharma teams with de novo miniprotein or binder programs approaching IND, and design-tool vendors who want immunogenicity data as proof of quality.
problem: Trend chain: AI binder design is cheap and abundant. Designs are entering the clinic (a de novo PD-L1 miniprotein has reached first-in-human imaging). But de novo proteins have no germline or humanization playbook, in silico epitope predictors over-call risk, and ex vivo T-cell panels are custom studies at CROs. PBMC vials cost about $460 each, so early-stage designers skip the test until a late failure.
solution: Bulk-buy an HLA-typed donor PBMC bank (30-50 donors covering major alleles). Run 96-well T-cell activation and proliferation assays plus MHC-associated peptide analysis on batches of 20-100 candidates per week. Return per-sequence hotspot maps, feed AI deimmunization redesign, then retest. Publish calibration against known immunogenic and non-immunogenic clinical proteins.
why_now: AI-drug funding tops $6B in 2026, and frontier-lab designs hit about 27% in Adaptyv's blind test, so many de novo programs are heading toward IND. FDA's shift toward human-relevant in vitro methods favors ex vivo immunogenicity assays.
revenue_model: $2-5k per candidate at batch scale, $50-150k for full deimmunization campaigns, and platform subscriptions for design companies.
non_obvious_insight: The cost driver is donors, not reagents. Buying donor lots at scale and running big plate batches flips the economics from 'per-molecule custom study' to 'per plate'. Every screen also calibrates the predictors that AI designers will later pay for, which builds a data flywheel.
first_30_days: Contract an existing immunology lab staffed by ex-CRO scientists. Order 30 HLA-typed PBMC lots at bulk pricing. Test 10 published de novo binders and 5 clinical reference proteins. Publish a preprint and pitch 10 protein-design startups.

title: Camera-to-Courtroom Evidence Provenance for Small Firms
one_liner: A capture app and export service that timestamps and cryptographically signs photos, video, texts and voicemails at collection, packaged with an authentication affidavit for court.
customer: Family-law, employment, landlord-tenant and personal-injury firms with up to 10 attorneys, their clients, legal-aid groups and HR investigators.
problem: Deepfakes make every screenshot and clip attackable. Courts and rule-makers are debating standards for machine-generated and possibly fabricated evidence (background, verify), and opposing counsel increasingly says 'that could be AI'. Honest clients then need a forensic expert at thousands of dollars per item to prove authenticity.
solution: Mobile capture that uses C2PA Content Credentials where phones support them (Pixel 10 added camera-level signing in 2025, background, verify) with a fallback for other devices, an SMS, WhatsApp and iMessage exporter with hash chaining, RFC 3161 trusted timestamps, chain-of-custody logs, and a one-click authentication package with a declaration template and a verifier page for the court. Optional expert-declaration add-on.
why_now: Mainstream phones gained hardware-backed provenance in 2025, judicial scrutiny of AI-generated evidence rose through 2025-26, and timestamping and signing infrastructure is now near-free.
revenue_model: $9-29 per case pack, $99-299/month per firm, and $250-500 per expert add-on.
non_obvious_insight: The generative-AI problem for law is not only fake evidence getting in, but real evidence being dismissed. Provenance at creation is a right-of-reply tool for the party with fewer resources, so the customer is the weaker litigant's lawyer.
first_30_days: Ship the capture app and message exporter, pilot with 15 family-law solos, get a forensic examiner to co-sign the package and stage a mock authentication hearing with a law-school clinic. Charge $99/month afterward.

title: Harvest Inns: Motel Wings as Farm Crew Housing
one_liner: A hospitality-grade operator that master-leases wings of underused rural motels and sublets compliant beds, meals and transport to growers who cannot house H-2A crews.
customer: Fruit and vegetable growers and grower associations using H-2A labor in Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Washington and Florida. The supply side is independent rural motels and extended-stay properties.
problem: Housing is the binding constraint on legally staffing harvests. Farm crews shrank after the immigration crackdown (up to 30% of strawberry and almond crews lost in Q1 2026), grapes, blueberries and peaches rotted unpicked in 2025, and H-2A jobs are heading toward 500K. Growers do not want to run hotels, and motel owners do not want H-2A paperwork while their occupancy stays weak in a K-shaped market.
solution: Master-lease 20-40 room wings for 10-16 weeks. Run the compliance layer: DOL public-accommodation rules (50 sq ft per person, 36-inch bed spacing, cooking and laundry ratios, direct payment by the employer to housing management), pre-built state workforce agency inspection files, linens and cleaning, catered or kitchenette meals and van shuttles. Software rebooks the same crews' beds in the next county as harvest calendars move, like a hotel chain whose guests are harvest crews. Inspection-first and worker-first standards are the moat.
why_now: DOL rules explicitly allow hotels and motels as H-2A housing, with local health codes applying first. The October 2025 wage-rule change and H-2A growth mean more growers are entering a system they have never staffed. Late crews and unpicked fields are now widely reported, and lower-tier hotels are under pressure while luxury leads.
revenue_model: Growers pay roughly $22-$35 per bed-night all-in (assumption to validate), of which motels get about $12-$20. Operator margin of 20-30% plus meal and transport upsells, sold as season contracts through grower associations.
non_obvious_insight: The idle asset already exists in every farm county, and the missing party is a specialist workforce-lodging operator, the ag version of oil-field man camps, who will absorb compliance risk. Motel owners value a guaranteed off-OTA base load more than a higher rate.
first_30_days: Pick one cluster such as south Georgia blueberries and peaches or Michigan cherries. Sign 3 motels for wings of 20-40 rooms, map the state inspection process with the workforce agency, and pre-sell 2 growers before March for the spring 2027 harvest season.

title: Outsourced Elder-Exploitation Desk for Credit Unions
one_liner: A managed service where trained specialists take flagged older-member transactions, call the member and trusted contact, file reports and document compliance.
customer: Community banks and credit unions ($300M-$5B in assets) with older memberships. Sales run through CUSOs, state leagues and core-processor marketplaces to BSA and fraud officers.
problem: Americans 60+ reported $7.7B in fraud losses in 2025 (up 59%), with an average loss over $38k and 12,400+ people losing $100k or more. Small institutions have alerts but no trained humans to call members, coordinate lawful holds, file SARs and APS reports, and prove Senior Safe Act training.
solution: Ingest the institution's flagged-alert queue and staff a desk with retired bank fraud investigators and social workers who use scripts to break the scam spell (pig-butchering, crypto-ATM, impostor). The desk coordinates holds, files APS and SAR narratives, runs annual Senior Safe Act training, and delivers quarterly avoided-loss analytics.
why_now: Investment and pig-butchering fraud is over a third of losses, older adults are adopting AI fast (23% of 65+ use ChatGPT, up from 10%), and voice-cloning scams raise stakes. State attorneys general and regulators are pressing institutions to do more.
revenue_model: $2-6k a month per institution by asset size, plus per-case fees, sold on documented avoided loss.
non_obvious_insight: Consumer fraud apps are crowded, but the institution is the party with a duty of care, and the missing capacity is human case handling, not another detection model. Pricing to avoided losses makes the ROI obvious.
first_30_days: Sell a 90-day pilot to two credit unions through a CUSO or state league, staffed by two retired fraud investigators and a social worker. Record prevented losses and hold-to-report cycle time.

title: 48-Hour Takedown Desk for Small Platforms
one_liner: A hosted notice-and-removal service that lets small user-content platforms meet the TAKE IT DOWN Act's 48-hour clock while filtering out weaponized false claims.
customer: Small and mid-size platforms hosting user content: niche forums, community and chat servers, creator and fan-content sites, marketplaces with seller photos, dating apps, and indie AI image and video generators. They pay $99-$2,000/month.
problem: Since 19 May 2026, covered platforms must run a removal process and take down non-consensual intimate imagery, including deepfakes and known identical copies, within 48 hours of a valid request. The FTC is enforcing, has sent warning letters to a dozen sites of varying sizes and can seek penalties above $50k per violation. Small teams cannot staff weekends or nights. The statute has no counter-notice or penalty for false claims, so bad-faith takedown floods by rivals or harassers are a real censorship tool.
solution: A drop-in intake page, API and email alias. Requesters are identity-verified and their signed statement is captured. Trained reviewers work 24/7 with a 4-hour internal target. Hash and perceptual matching (including StopNCII) finds copies across the customer's site. The desk executes removals, logs evidence and produces a monthly FTC-ready compliance report. A shared claimant-reputation graph flags serial or coordinated false claimants across customers, with configurable reinstatement policies.
why_now: Enforcement is live and visibly reaching small sites. AI image generators multiply NCII volume. Small platforms that could ignore trust and safety until now have a hard federal clock.
revenue_model: Subscription tiered by monthly active users and case volume, plus a per-case fee above quota. Enterprise plans for AI image and video generators, and an add-on for FTC inquiry support.
non_obvious_insight: Detection is not the scarce resource, since StopNCII and hashing already exist. The scarce resources are accountable human judgment on a 48-hour clock and cross-platform intelligence on abusive claimants, which only a shared vendor can see. The law's missing abuse safeguard is the product.
first_30_days: Build intake and workflow on Retool or Airtable with 6 ex-trust-and-safety reviewers across two time zones. Contact 100 small platforms found via FTC warning-letter coverage and forum and community host lists, offering a 30-day free pilot. Publish a free compliance checklist for lead capture, then charge $199/month from the second month.

title: Royalty Marketplace for Expert Agent Skills
one_liner: Retired and displaced specialists package their procedures, judgment rubrics and worked examples as machine-loadable skill packs that companies' agents pull on demand, with per-run metering and royalties to the author.
customer: Enterprises and SMBs deploying agents in regulated or technical workflows pay $200-2,000 a month per seat or per run. Authors are displaced experts who earn royalties.
problem: Agents are competent generalists that fail on domain procedures (customs classification, prior-authorisation appeals, tax-exchange steps). Hourly expert gigs pay once, so expertise is consumed without ongoing income, and enterprises can't find vetted, tested procedures.
solution: A curated marketplace of skill packs in the open Agent Skills format (instructions, scripts and tests), each with an eval suite and author credentials, metered per invocation through an MCP gateway. Quality is scored on held-out test performance and versions update as rules change. Wedge: tariff and customs-compliance packs written by retired customs brokers.
why_now: The Agent Skills format (Oct 2025) and MCP are becoming standard across agent tools, tariff volatility since 2025 has created urgent demand for trade-compliance expertise, and experienced professionals are being displaced.
revenue_model: 25-30% take on subscriptions and per-run fees, plus enterprise private-skill hosting.
non_obvious_insight: Hourly data labor turns experts into a consumable, while royalties make them asset owners. A metered gateway makes value attributable, and the moat is trusted eval suites rather than the marketplace itself.
first_30_days: Recruit 8 retired customs brokers or trade-compliance professionals. Build 5 tested skill packs and an eval harness. Sell to 10 importers already using agents at $300 a month and measure error reduction.

title: Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls
one_liner: A contingency-fee service that finds and files the warranty claims on energized-but-empty data halls before OEM warranty clocks silently expire.
customer: Colocation developers, powered-shell landlords, neocloud operators and enterprise owners with phased or delayed-tenant builds, especially those with halls commissioned 6-14 months ago and not yet loaded. The owner pays a percentage of recovered value, plus an optional per-asset tracking subscription.
problem: Warranty clocks on generators, UPS systems, chillers, CRAH/CDUs, switchgear, and batteries usually start at shipment or startup, not when a tenant loads the hall. With delayed leases and mid-build AI redesigns, halls sit energized and idle for months. Many defects only show under real load (UPS capacitors, chiller compressors, wet-stacking gensets, breaker trip curves, coolant chemistry). By the time the tenant ramps, the warranty has expired. The turnover package is 50,000+ pages of PDFs that ops never reads, the punch-list deferrals are lost, and OEM maintenance records required to keep coverage valid are often missing. Nobody owns the clock.
solution: Ingest POs, OEM warranty terms, startup sheets, Cx reports, shipping documents and maintenance logs with an LLM pipeline to build a serial-number-level warranty ledger with real expiry dates and voiding conditions. Flag anything expiring within 120 days. Run a targeted load-dependent-defect inspection before expiry (thermography, oil and coolant samples, capacitor and battery checks, breaker testing). File claims, negotiate warranty start-date deferrals or extensions with the OEM while leverage still exists, and fix missing maintenance-record gaps. For new builds, sell a PO-stage clause pack that defers warranty start to beneficial occupancy.
why_now: There is a glut of speculative shells and delayed tenant handoffs. Reporting in 2026 shows close to half of planned US builds slipping, with only about a third of 2026 target capacity under active construction. That means many halls are powered, commissioned and idle. Equipment was bought at peak prices with tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper, so each lapsed warranty is worth more. LLMs can now read messy closeout binders cheaply, which was the labor bottleneck for audits like this.
revenue_model: 25-30% of recovered value or avoided cost on claims and negotiated extensions, no fee if nothing is recovered. Optional $150-400 per asset per year tracking subscription. $15K-40K fixed-fee closeout audits for owners who want certainty. PO-stage clause-pack consulting for developers.
non_obvious_insight: The warranty is the only major asset on a data center balance sheet that expires silently. OEMs will defer warranty start dates at PO time, but almost no one negotiates it because the project team is fighting for delivery slots, not paperwork. After the fact, the owner's ops team inherits the docs with no idea when the clocks started. The money is in the punch-list items that were 'to be fixed later' and the load-dependent defects that only appear after the hall is finally used.
first_30_days: Find 3 owner-operators through PM and Cx network contacts with halls energized 8-11 months ago and not fully loaded. Offer a free 10-day scan of their closeout binders in exchange for a contingency agreement on any claims. Build the extraction pipeline on real binders (gensets, UPS, chillers first). Deliver a 'expiring within 90 days' hit list and file the first claims before the first invoice.

title: Human-Review Receipts for the EU Text Exemption
one_liner: Sell signed proof that a named human reviewed and took responsibility for AI-assisted text, which is the thing the EU's disclosure rule for text appears to reward, not labels on AI.
customer: Newsletter operators, niche and local publishers, and B2B content agencies that publish AI-assisted text to EU readers. Second buyers are legal and compliance leads at mid-market publishers.
problem: The industry reads EU AI Act Art. 50 (applicable Aug 2, 2026) as 'label the AI.' My understanding of Art. 50(4) is that the text-disclosure duty for public-interest publications has an exemption where content underwent human review or editorial control and a person holds editorial responsibility. Confirm the exact wording with counsel, because the brief does not quote it. Meanwhile readers get accusation tools: Substack embedded Pangram scanning on Jul 22 and LinkedIn added a slop-report button on Jul 30. Publishers have no defensible record of human review.
solution: A Ghost, WordPress and Substack-compatible plugin plus API that records, per article, the AI draft versus the final diff, who reviewed it, and a passkey-signed approval bound to the content hash. It publishes a verification page and a byline element ('reviewed and edited by [name]'), and generates an evidence binder for regulators and clients. If no review is recorded, it falls back to an automatic disclosure line.
why_now: Art. 50 became applicable on Aug 2, 2026, and reader-side detection has just been built into major platforms. The first regulatory questions and client audits will land on publishers this year.
revenue_model: $29-99/month per publication, $500-2,000/month agency plans, and $250 per audit-ready evidence binder.
non_obvious_insight: Detection tries to prove a negative ('not AI'). The law's structure turns human review into a legal safe harbor, so the sellable product is a positive: a named person accepted responsibility. That gives 'human-made' a compliance budget instead of an ethics budget.
first_30_days: Ship a Ghost/WordPress plugin with diff capture and passkey sign-off in about three weeks. Approach 10 EU-facing newsletters and 3 agencies with 'Aug 2 has passed, where is your evidence?' Co-brand the evidence binder with one EU tech-law boutique that can use it as a channel.

title: Subsurface Desert Mapping From Free Radar Satellites
one_liner: Use open L-band radar data to map buried channels and structures beneath arid ground for mineral and water explorers.
customer: Junior critical-mineral explorers, uranium and lithium prospectors, groundwater drillers, national geological surveys and arid-region water utilities.
problem: Exploration in deserts costs a fortune per drill hole, targeting is often guesswork, and airborne geophysics is expensive. Explorers need cheaper first-pass targeting.
solution: Combine weekly-repeat NISAR L-band radar (open data), Sentinel-1 and, outside North America and Europe, ESA Biomass P-band to map buried paleo-channels, faults and shallow structure in hyper-arid terrain. Deliver target packages per license block, plus a success-fee option.
why_now: NISAR launched in July 2025 with an open-data policy, and ESA's Biomass P-band radar launched in April 2025. Demand for critical minerals is at a peak. Radar penetration only works in very dry ground, so scope is narrow but valuable.
revenue_model: $20-60k per license block. Success fee or royalty on discoveries. Annual subscriptions for geological surveys.
non_obvious_insight: Seeing beneath sand from orbit sounds like science fiction, and it is now possible with free data. The business is expertise and interpretation, not satellites.
first_30_days: Pick two well-studied arid areas as proof cases and reproduce known buried channels. Show results to 20 junior explorers with licenses in arid regions. Sell the first two block packages at a discount for case studies.
